strings.b-00-meta.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can describe the magnetic field of a magnet and list the properties of magnetic field lines.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can find the direction of the magnetic field produced by a current in a straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid using the right-hand thumb rule.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.3: After this lesson you can explain the live, neutral and earth wires of a domestic circuit, and why a fuse protects the circuit from short-circuiting and overloading.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: The region around a magnet in which the force of the magnet can be detected.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: The line along which iron filings line up around a magnet; a compass needle placed on it points along its direction.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: A rule for the direction of the field around a straight current-carrying wire: thumb along the current, curled fingers along the field.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: A rule for the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor: forefinger along the field, second finger along the current, thumb along the force.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: A coil of many circular turns wound in the shape of a cylinder, whose field is like that of a bar magnet.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: A soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire, made magnetic by passing a current through the coil.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when too large a current flows, protecting appliances from damage.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: A fault in which the live wire and the neutral wire touch directly, so the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.8.definition: The green-insulated safety wire connected to a metal plate in the earth, which keeps a metallic appliance body at the earth's potential.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: You already know one effect of an electric current: it heats the wire it flows through. There is a second effect. A wire carrying a current also behaves like a magnet, and you can see this with a compass.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: Take a thick straight copper wire and connect it between two points, X and Y, of an electric circuit. Keep the wire perpendicular to the plane of the paper. Place a small compass horizontally near the wire and note the position of its needle.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: Now insert the key so that current flows, and look at the needle again. The needle is deflected. The electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. Electricity and magnetism are linked to each other.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.3: This link was found by accident. In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted discovered that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby. His observation showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena.
strings.b-02.question: Why does a compass needle get deflected when it is brought near a bar magnet?
strings.b-02.options.0: The magnet's field exerts a force on the needle, because the needle is itself a small magnet.
strings.b-02.options.1: The magnet attracts only the glass cover of the compass, not the needle.
strings.b-02.options.2: The needle is made of copper, which is attracted by any magnet.
strings.b-02.options.3: The magnet heats the needle, and heat makes the needle turn.
strings.b-02.explanation: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. A bar magnet produces a magnetic field around itself, and inside that field a force acts on another magnet, so the needle turns.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.0: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. Its two ends point approximately towards the north and south directions. The end that points towards the north is called the north-seeking or north pole; the other end, which points towards the south, is called the south-seeking or south pole. Like poles repel each other, and unlike poles attract each other.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.1: Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board. Place a bar magnet in the centre and sprinkle iron filings uniformly around it. Tap the board gently. The iron filings arrange themselves in a pattern.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.2: Why do they arrange in a pattern? The magnet exerts its influence in the region around it, and the filings experience a force. The region surrounding a magnet in which the force of the magnet can be detected is said to have a magnetic field. The lines along which the iron filings align themselves represent magnetic field lines.
strings.b-04.caption: Field lines around a bar magnet. The arrowheads show the convention: lines come out of the north pole, curve round outside the magnet and go into the south pole, so every line is a closed curve. The lines are crowded near the poles, where the field is strongest.
strings.b-05.paragraphs.0: Four properties follow. First, the direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction in which a north pole of the compass needle would move there. By convention, field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole, and inside the magnet their direction is from the south pole to the north pole, so field lines are closed curves.
strings.b-05.paragraphs.1: Second, the relative strength of the field is shown by the degree of closeness of the lines: the field is stronger where the lines are crowded. Third, no two field lines cross each other, because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
strings.b-05.paragraphs.2: Fourth, the deflection of the needle increases as it is moved along a field line towards the poles.
strings.b-06.title: How to draw one magnetic field line with a compass
strings.b-06.steps.0.title: Set up
strings.b-06.steps.0.detail: Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board, place the bar magnet on it and mark the boundary of the magnet.
strings.b-06.steps.1.title: First position
strings.b-06.steps.1.detail: Place the compass near the north pole of the magnet. The south pole of the needle points towards the north pole of the magnet, and the north pole of the compass is directed away from the magnet's north pole. Mark the positions of the two ends of the needle.
strings.b-06.steps.2.title: Step along
strings.b-06.steps.2.detail: Move the needle to a new position such that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole.
strings.b-06.steps.3.title: Continue to the south pole
strings.b-06.steps.3.detail: Proceed step by step in this way until you reach the south pole of the magnet.
strings.b-06.steps.4.title: Join the marks
strings.b-06.steps.4.detail: Join the points marked on the paper by a smooth curve. This curve represents a field line.
strings.b-06.steps.5.title: Repeat
strings.b-06.steps.5.detail: Repeat the whole procedure and draw as many lines as you can. Together they represent the magnetic field around the magnet.
strings.b-07.question: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
strings.b-07.options.0: Because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
strings.b-07.options.1: Because field lines are always straight and straight lines never meet.
strings.b-07.options.2: Because the magnetic field is zero at every crossing point.
strings.b-07.options.3: Because field lines exist only inside the magnet.
strings.b-07.explanation: The direction of the field at a point is the direction in which the north pole of a compass needle would move there. A single point cannot give two directions, so two field lines cannot cross.
strings.b-08.question: Which two methods of producing a magnetic field are shown in this chapter?
strings.b-08.options.0: By using a magnet, and by passing an electric current through a conductor.
strings.b-08.options.1: By heating a wire, and by cooling a magnet.
strings.b-08.options.2: By rubbing a copper wire, and by breaking a magnet into pieces.
strings.b-08.options.3: By shining light on a wire, and by making a loud sound.
strings.b-08.explanation: A magnetic field exists in the region surrounding a magnet, and a metallic wire carrying an electric current also has a magnetic field associated with it.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.0: What decides the pattern of the magnetic field generated by a current through a conductor? The pattern depends on the shape of the conductor. Start with a long straight wire.
strings.b-09.paragraphs.1: Take a long straight copper wire, two or three cells of 1.5 V each and a plug key, and connect them in series. Place the straight wire parallel to and over a compass needle, then plug in the key. If the current flows from north to south, the north pole of the compass needle moves towards the east. Now replace the cell connections so that the current flows from south to north; the needle moves towards the west. The direction of the magnetic field is reversed when the current is reversed.
strings.b-10.caption: The field of a straight current-carrying wire, seen by looking along the wire: the field lines are concentric circles centred on the wire, and they become larger and larger as we move away. The arrowheads show the direction of the field for a current coming out of the page.
strings.b-10.svg_texts.t-0: wire seen end-on; current coming out of the page
strings.b-11.paragraphs.0: Two more facts come from the same experiment. If you increase the current in the wire, the deflection of the needle increases; so the magnitude of the magnetic field at a given point increases as the current through the wire increases.
strings.b-11.paragraphs.1: If you keep the current the same but move the compass farther from the wire, the deflection decreases; so the field produced by a given current decreases as the distance from the wire increases. The concentric circles representing the field become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.
strings.b-12.question: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire carrying a current?
strings.b-12.options.0: The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.
strings.b-12.options.1: The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.
strings.b-12.options.2: The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.
strings.b-12.options.3: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
strings.b-12.explanation: Iron filings sprinkled around a straight current-carrying wire arrange themselves in concentric circles around the wire, and these circles represent the field lines.
strings.b-13.paragraphs.0: Here is a convenient way to remember the direction of the field around a straight current-carrying conductor. Imagine that you are holding the conductor in your right hand such that your thumb points towards the direction of the current. Your fingers then wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines. This is the right-hand thumb rule.
strings.b-13.paragraphs.1: The same rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule: if you consider yourself driving a corkscrew in the direction of the current, then the direction of rotation of the corkscrew is the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-14.problem: A current through a horizontal power line flows in the east to west direction. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?
strings.b-14.steps.0.title: Point the thumb
strings.b-14.steps.0.detail: Hold the power line in your right hand so that your thumb points along the current, that is, from east to west.
strings.b-14.steps.1.title: Curl the fingers
strings.b-14.steps.1.detail: Your fingers wrap around the wire. They give the direction of the field lines in a plane perpendicular to the wire.
strings.b-14.steps.2.title: Look from one end
strings.b-14.steps.2.detail: Viewed from the east end, this curling is clockwise; viewed from the west end it is anti-clockwise.
strings.b-14.steps.3.title: Same above and below
strings.b-14.steps.3.detail: Nothing changes at a point directly below or directly above the wire: the field still turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.
strings.b-14.answer: At any point directly below or directly above the wire, the magnetic field turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.
strings.b-15.question: Which rule gives the direction of the magnetic field produced around a straight current-carrying conductor?
strings.b-15.options.0: The right-hand thumb rule, also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule.
strings.b-15.options.1: The rule that a compass needle points north.
strings.b-15.options.2: The rule that like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
strings.b-15.options.3: The rule that iron filings settle in straight lines.
strings.b-15.explanation: Hold the current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the current. Your fingers then wrap around the conductor in the direction of the magnetic field lines.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.0: Now bend that straight wire into a circular loop and pass a current through it. The magnetic field of a straight wire depends inversely on the distance from it; in the same way, at every point of a current-carrying circular loop the concentric circles representing the field become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.1: By the time we reach the centre of the loop, the arcs of these big circles appear as straight lines. Every point on the wire carrying current gives rise to a magnetic field that appears as a straight line at the centre of the loop. Applying the right-hand rule shows that every section of the wire contributes to the magnetic field lines in the same direction within the loop.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.2: The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire at a given point depends directly on the current passing through it. So if a circular coil has n turns, the field produced is n times as large as that produced by a single turn: the current in each circular turn has the same direction, and the fields due to the turns just add up.
strings.b-17.caption: A circular loop carrying current in the clockwise direction. The crossed circle at the centre marks the field B, which is perpendicular to the plane of the loop and points into the page; at the centre the field lines appear as straight lines.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.0: A solenoid is a coil with many circular turns wound in the shape of a cylinder. The pattern of the magnetic field lines through and around a current-carrying solenoid is similar to that of a bar magnet, and one end of the solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole. Inside a long straight solenoid carrying current, the magnetic field is the same at all points.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.1: A current-carrying solenoid coil is used to magnetise a steel rod placed inside it. This arrangement is an electromagnet. An electromagnet consists of a core of soft iron wrapped around with a coil of insulated copper wire.
strings.b-19.question: Choose the correct option. The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid carrying current
strings.b-19.options.1: decreases as we move towards its end.
strings.b-19.options.2: increases as we move towards its end.
strings.b-19.options.3: is the same at all points.
strings.b-19.explanation: Inside a long straight solenoid carrying current the field lines are parallel and the field is uniform, so the field is the same at all points inside it.
strings.b-20.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines.
strings.b-20.explanation: At the centre of a current-carrying circular coil the arcs of the big circles appear as straight lines, and every section of the wire contributes in the same direction there, so the field lines at the centre are parallel straight lines.
strings.b-21.question: A circular loop of wire lies in the plane of the table and the current in it flows clockwise, as seen from above. Applying the right-hand rule, the magnetic field at the centre of the loop is directed
strings.b-21.options.0: into the table, perpendicular to the plane of the table.
strings.b-21.options.1: out of the table, perpendicular to the plane of the table.
strings.b-21.options.2: along the table, towards the north.
strings.b-21.options.3: along the wire itself, round the loop.
strings.b-21.explanation: Curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of the current, that is clockwise; your thumb then points into the table. Inside the loop every section of the wire contributes its field in that same direction.
strings.b-22.paragraphs.0: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field, and that field exerts a force on a magnet placed near the conductor. The French scientist Andre Marie Ampere suggested that the magnet must also exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor.
strings.b-22.paragraphs.1: Take a small aluminium rod AB of about 5 cm and suspend it horizontally from a stand using two connecting wires. Place a strong horse-shoe magnet so that the rod lies between its two poles with the magnetic field directed upwards: north pole vertically below and south pole vertically above the rod. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat, and pass a current through the rod from end B to end A. The rod is displaced towards the left. Reverse the direction of the current and the rod is displaced towards the right.
strings.b-22.paragraphs.2: Now change the direction of the field to vertically downwards by interchanging the two poles of the magnet. The direction of the force acting on the current-carrying rod is reversed again. So the direction of the force depends on the direction of the current and on the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-23.caption: The rod AB is drawn as a small circle because it points straight out of the page towards you; the dot in it marks a current coming out of the page. The magnetic field B points upwards (north pole below, south pole above), so the force F on the rod is perpendicular to both and points to the left. The arrows show directions only.
strings.b-24.paragraphs.0: The displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the magnitude of the force is highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field. In such a condition a simple rule gives the direction of the force.
strings.b-24.paragraphs.1: Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand such that they are mutually perpendicular. If the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of motion or the force acting on the conductor.
strings.b-24.paragraphs.2: Remember that the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, the electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.
strings.b-25.problem: An electron moves horizontally towards the east and enters a magnetic field that points vertically upwards, at right angles to its motion. In which direction does the force acting on the electron point?
strings.b-25.steps.0.title: Fix the field direction
strings.b-25.steps.0.detail: The magnetic field points vertically upwards, so the forefinger of the left hand points up.
strings.b-25.steps.1.title: Find the current direction
strings.b-25.steps.1.detail: The electron moves towards the east. The direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons, so the current is towards the west. The second finger points west.
strings.b-25.steps.2.title: Read the thumb
strings.b-25.steps.2.detail: With the forefinger up and the second finger pointing west, the thumb of the left hand points towards the north.
strings.b-25.steps.3.title: State the result
strings.b-25.steps.3.detail: The force acts perpendicular to both the field and the current, so it is directed horizontally towards the north.
strings.b-25.answer: The force on the electron acts towards the north.
strings.b-26.question: A positively charged alpha-particle projected towards the west is deflected towards the north by a magnetic field. The direction of the magnetic field is
strings.b-26.explanation: An alpha-particle is positively charged, so the current is towards the west. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the thumb must point north (the force) and the second finger west (the current); the forefinger then points upward, which is the direction of the field.
strings.b-27.question: An electron moves horizontally towards the east. In which direction is the electric current taken?
strings.b-27.explanation: The direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. Since the electron moves towards the east, the current is taken towards the west.
strings.b-28.question: You are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam moving horizontally from the back wall towards the front wall is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
strings.b-28.explanation: The electrons move towards the front wall, so the current is taken in the opposite direction, towards the back wall. The force is to your right. With Fleming's left-hand rule, the thumb points right and the second finger points towards the back wall; the forefinger then points vertically downwards.
strings.b-29.question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
strings.b-29.options.0: When the current is parallel to the magnetic field.
strings.b-29.options.1: When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
strings.b-29.options.2: When the current in the conductor is zero.
strings.b-29.options.3: When the conductor is kept outside the magnetic field.
strings.b-29.explanation: The displacement of the rod in the activity, and so the magnitude of the force, is largest when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-30.question: In Activity 12.7, the direction of the force acting on the current-carrying rod depends on which of the following?
strings.b-30.options.0: Only the direction of the current.
strings.b-30.options.1: Only the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-30.options.2: Both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-30.options.3: Neither; the force has a fixed direction.
strings.b-30.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the direction of displacement, and changing the direction of the magnetic field by interchanging the poles also reverses the force. So the force direction depends on both the current direction and the field direction.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.0: Electric power reaches a house through a main supply, either supported through overhead electric poles or by underground cables. One wire of this supply, usually with red insulation, is called the live wire (or positive). Another wire, with black insulation, is called the neutral wire (or negative). In our country the potential difference between the two is 220 V.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.1: At the meter-board in the house these wires pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse, and through a main switch they are connected to the line wires in the house. Often two separate circuits are used: one of 15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as geysers and air coolers, and the other of 5 A current rating for bulbs and fans.
strings.b-31.paragraphs.2: The earth wire has insulation of green colour and is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. It is a safety measure, especially for appliances that have a metallic body, for example an electric press, a toaster, a table fan or a refrigerator. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Any leakage of current to the metallic body then keeps its potential equal to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
strings.b-32.caption: One common domestic circuit. The bulb circuit and the appliance are both connected across the live and neutral wires, so they are in parallel and each gets the same potential difference; each has its own switch. The appliance's metal body is joined to the earth wire. Where lines cross without a dot there is no connection.
strings.b-33.paragraphs.0: In each separate circuit, different appliances can be connected across the live and neutral wires, and each appliance has a separate switch to switch the current on and off. In order that each appliance has equal potential difference, the appliances are connected in parallel to each other.
strings.b-33.paragraphs.1: A fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. It prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact; this happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance. In such a situation the current in the circuit abruptly increases, and this is called short-circuiting. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it to break the electric circuit and stop the flow of an unduly high current.
strings.b-33.paragraphs.2: Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, and sometimes it is caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.
strings.b-34.problem: In a domestic circuit, the insulation of a wire gets damaged and the live wire comes into direct contact with the neutral wire. Explain what happens in the circuit and what the fuse does.
strings.b-34.steps.0.title: Direct contact
strings.b-34.steps.0.detail: The live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact. This is called short-circuiting.
strings.b-34.steps.1.title: Current increases
strings.b-34.steps.1.detail: Because of this direct contact, the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
strings.b-34.steps.2.title: Fuse heats
strings.b-34.steps.2.detail: The unduly high current causes Joule heating in the fuse.
strings.b-34.steps.3.title: Circuit breaks
strings.b-34.steps.3.detail: The Joule heating melts the fuse, which breaks the electric circuit and stops the flow of the unduly high current, preventing damage to the appliances and the circuit.
strings.b-34.answer: The damaged insulation causes short-circuiting: the live and neutral wires touch, the current abruptly increases, and the Joule heating melts the fuse, which breaks the circuit and prevents damage.
strings.b-35.question: At the time of a short circuit, the current in the circuit
strings.b-35.explanation: When the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact, the current in the circuit abruptly increases; this is called short-circuiting.
strings.b-36.question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
strings.b-36.options.0: When the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact.
strings.b-36.options.1: When the earth wire is connected to a metal plate in the ground.
strings.b-36.options.2: When too many appliances are switched off at the same time.
strings.b-36.options.3: When the supply voltage falls below 220 V.
strings.b-36.explanation: This happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance, and then the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
strings.b-37.question: What is the function of an earth wire, and why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
strings.b-37.options.0: It provides a low-resistance conducting path, so any leakage of current to the metallic body keeps its potential at that of the earth and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
strings.b-37.options.1: It carries the working current to the appliance in place of the live wire.
strings.b-37.options.2: It increases the current in the circuit so that the appliance works faster.
strings.b-37.options.3: It converts the alternating supply into direct current for the appliance.
strings.b-37.explanation: The earth wire is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth. When the metallic body of an appliance is joined to it, a leakage current is taken safely to the earth instead of through the user.
strings.b-38.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
strings.b-38.explanation: The wire with green insulation is the earth wire. The live wire usually has red insulation and the neutral wire has black insulation.
strings.b-39.question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
strings.b-39.options.0: The electric fuse and the earth wire.
strings.b-39.explanation: The fuse melts and breaks the circuit when the current is unduly high, and the earth wire takes leakage current safely to the earth.
strings.b-40.question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
strings.b-40.options.0: Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket, and do not draw more current than the circuit's rating.
strings.b-40.options.1: Connect all the appliances of the house in series.
strings.b-40.options.2: Remove the fuse from the main board.
strings.b-40.options.3: Disconnect the earth wire from the metallic appliances.
strings.b-40.explanation: Overloading can be caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket, and also by an accidental hike in the supply voltage; the fuse is there to break the circuit if it happens.
strings.b-41.paragraphs.0: An electric current always produces a magnetic field. Even the weak ion currents that travel along the nerve cells in our body produce magnetic fields. When you touch something, your nerves carry an electric impulse to the muscles you need to use, and this impulse produces a temporary magnetic field. Such fields are very weak, about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field.
strings.b-41.paragraphs.1: The two main organs in the human body where the magnetic field produced is significant are the heart and the brain. The magnetic field inside the body forms the basis of obtaining images of different body parts by a technique called Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.
strings.b-42.question: Which technique uses the magnetic field inside the human body to obtain images of different body parts?
strings.b-42.explanation: The magnetic field inside the body, which is significant in the heart and the brain, is the basis of obtaining images of body parts by MRI, and analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.

lesson.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
objectives: After this lesson you can describe the magnetic field of a magnet and list the properties of magnetic field lines.
After this lesson you can find the direction of the magnetic field produced by a current in a straight wire, a circular loop and a solenoid using the right-hand thumb rule.
After this lesson you can use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
After this lesson you can explain the live, neutral and earth wires of a domestic circuit, and why a fuse protects the circuit from short-circuiting and overloading.

sections.title: A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet
paragraphs: You already know one effect of an electric current: it heats the wire it flows through. There is a second effect. A wire carrying a current also behaves like a magnet, and you can see this with a compass.

Take a thick straight copper wire and connect it between two points, X and Y, of an electric circuit. Keep the wire perpendicular to the plane of the paper. Place a small compass horizontally near the wire and note the position of its needle.

Now insert the key so that current flows, and look at the needle again. The needle is deflected. The electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. Electricity and magnetism are linked to each other.

This link was found by accident. In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted discovered that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby. His observation showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena.

In this lesson you will learn how a current produces a magnetic field, how to find the direction of that field, how a magnet exerts a force on a current-carrying conductor, and how the electric wiring of a house is arranged.

sections.title: Magnetic field and field lines
paragraphs: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. Its two ends point approximately towards the north and south directions. The end that points towards the north is called the north-seeking or north pole; the other end, which points towards the south, is called the south-seeking or south pole. Like poles repel each other, and unlike poles attract each other.

Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board. Place a bar magnet in the centre and sprinkle iron filings uniformly around it; a salt-sprinkler may be used. Tap the board gently. The iron filings arrange themselves in a pattern.

Why do they arrange in a pattern? The magnet exerts its influence in the region around it, and the filings experience a force. The region surrounding a magnet in which the force of the magnet can be detected is said to have a magnetic field. The lines along which the iron filings align themselves represent magnetic field lines.

You can draw these lines yourself with a small compass. Place the magnet on a sheet of paper fixed on a drawing board and mark the boundary of the magnet. Place the compass near the north pole of the magnet: the south pole of the needle points towards the north pole of the magnet, and the north pole of the compass is directed away from the magnet's north pole. Mark the positions of the two ends of the needle.

Now move the compass to a new position such that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole. Proceed step by step until you reach the south pole of the magnet. Join the marked points with a smooth curve. That curve is one field line. Repeat the procedure and draw as many lines as you can.

Four properties follow. First, the direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction in which a north pole of the compass needle would move there. By convention, field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole, and inside the magnet their direction is from the south pole to the north pole, so field lines are closed curves.

Second, the relative strength of the field is shown by the degree of closeness of the lines: the field is stronger where the lines are crowded. Third, no two field lines cross each other, because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible. Fourth, the deflection of the needle increases as it is moved along a field line towards the poles.

sections.title: Magnetic field due to a current through a straight conductor
paragraphs: What decides the pattern of the magnetic field generated by a current through a conductor? The pattern depends on the shape of the conductor. Start with a long straight wire.

Take a long straight copper wire, two or three cells of 1.5 V each and a plug key, and connect them in series. Place the straight wire parallel to and over a compass needle, then plug in the key. If the current flows from north to south, the north pole of the compass needle moves towards the east. Now replace the cell connections so that the current flows from south to north; the needle moves towards the west. The direction of the magnetic field is reversed when the current is reversed.

To see the shape of the field, pass a long thick straight copper wire through the centre of a rectangular cardboard, normal to its plane, and connect it in series with a 12 V battery, a variable resistance (rheostat), an ammeter and a plug key. Sprinkle iron filings on the cardboard, close the key, and tap the cardboard gently. The filings arrange themselves in a pattern of concentric circles around the copper wire, and these circles represent the magnetic field lines.
Place a compass at a point on one of the circles. The direction in which the north pole of the needle points gives the direction of the field line at that point.

Two more facts come from the same activity. If you increase the current in the wire, the deflection of the needle increases; so the magnitude of the magnetic field at a given point increases as the current through the wire increases. If you keep the current the same but move the compass farther from the wire, the deflection decreases; so the field produced by a given current decreases as the distance from the wire increases. The concentric circles become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.

sections.title: The right-hand thumb rule
paragraphs: Here is a convenient way to remember the direction of the field around a straight current-carrying conductor. Imagine that you are holding the conductor in your right hand such that your thumb points towards the direction of the current. Your fingers then wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines. This is the right-hand thumb rule.

The same rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule: if you think of yourself driving a corkscrew in the direction of the current, then the direction of rotation of the corkscrew is the direction of the magnetic field.

Here is the rule used on a real line. A current through a horizontal power line flows in the east to west direction. Hold the wire with your right thumb pointing from east to west and let your fingers curl around it. At any point directly below or directly above the wire, the field turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

sections.title: Magnetic field due to a current through a circular loop
paragraphs: Now bend that straight wire into a circular loop and pass a current through it. The magnetic field of a straight wire depends inversely on the distance from it; in the same way, at every point of a current-carrying circular loop the concentric circles representing the field become larger and larger as we move away from the wire.

By the time we reach the centre of the loop, the arcs of these big circles appear as straight lines. Every point on the wire carrying current gives rise to a magnetic field that appears as a straight line at the centre of the loop. Applying the right-hand rule shows that every section of the wire contributes to the magnetic field lines in the same direction within the loop.

The magnetic field produced by a current-carrying wire at a given point depends directly on the current passing through it. So if a circular coil has n turns, the field produced is n times as large as that produced by a single turn: the current in each circular turn has the same direction, and the fields due to the turns just add up.

A solenoid is a coil with many circular turns wound in the shape of a cylinder. The pattern of the magnetic field lines through and around a current-carrying solenoid is similar to that of a bar magnet, and one end of the solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole. Inside a long straight solenoid carrying current, the magnetic field is the same at all points.

A current-carrying solenoid coil is used to magnetise a steel rod placed inside it. This arrangement is an electromagnet. An electromagnet consists of a core of soft iron wrapped around with a coil of insulated copper wire.

sections.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
paragraphs: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field, and that field exerts a force on a magnet placed near the conductor. The French scientist Andre Marie Ampere suggested that the magnet must also exert an equal and opposite force on the current-carrying conductor.

Take a small aluminium rod AB of about 5 cm and suspend it horizontally from a stand using two connecting wires. Place a strong horse-shoe magnet so that the rod lies between its two poles with the magnetic field directed upwards: north pole vertically below and south pole vertically above the rod. Connect the rod in series with a battery, a key and a rheostat, and pass a current through the rod from end B to end A. The rod is displaced towards the left. Reverse the direction of the current and the rod is displaced towards the right.

Now change the direction of the field to vertically downwards by interchanging the two poles of the magnet. The direction of the force acting on the current-carrying rod is reversed again. So the direction of the force depends on the direction of the current and on the direction of the magnetic field.

The displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the magnitude of the force is highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field. In such a condition a simple rule gives the direction of the force.

Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand such that they are mutually perpendicular. If the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of motion or the force acting on the conductor.

Remember that the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, the electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.

sections.title: Domestic electric circuits
paragraphs: Electric power reaches a house through a main supply, either supported through overhead electric poles or by underground cables. One wire of this supply, usually with red insulation, is called the live wire (or positive). Another wire, with black insulation, is called the neutral wire (or negative). In our country the potential difference between the two is 220 V.

At the meter-board in the house these wires pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse, and through a main switch they are connected to the line wires in the house. Often two separate circuits are used: one of 15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as geysers and air coolers, and the other of 5 A current rating for bulbs and fans.

The earth wire has insulation of green colour and is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. It is a safety measure, especially for appliances that have a metallic body, for example an electric press, a toaster, a table fan or a refrigerator. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Any leakage of current to the metallic body then keeps its potential equal to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.

In each separate circuit, different appliances can be connected across the live and neutral wires, and each appliance has a separate switch to switch the current on and off. In order that each appliance has equal potential difference, the appliances are connected in parallel to each other.

A fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. It prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact; this happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance. In such a situation the current in the circuit abruptly increases, and this is called short-circuiting. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it to break the electric circuit and stop the flow of an unduly high current.
Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, and sometimes it is caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.

sections.title: Magnetism in medicine
paragraphs: An electric current always produces a magnetic field. Even the weak ion currents that travel along the nerve cells in our body produce magnetic fields. When you touch something, your nerves carry an electric impulse to the muscles you need to use, and this impulse produces a temporary magnetic field. Such fields are very weak, about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field.

The two main organs in the human body where the magnetic field produced is significant are the heart and the brain. The magnetic field inside the body forms the basis of obtaining images of different body parts by a technique called Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.

spec.title: How to draw one magnetic field line with a compass

steps.title: Set up
steps.detail: Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board, place the bar magnet on it and mark the boundary of the magnet.

steps.title: First position
steps.detail: Place the compass near the north pole of the magnet. The south pole of the needle points towards the north pole of the magnet, and the north pole of the compass is directed away from the magnet's north pole. Mark the positions of the two ends of the needle.

steps.title: Step along
steps.detail: Move the needle to a new position such that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole.

steps.title: Continue to the south pole
steps.detail: Proceed step by step in this way until you reach the south pole of the magnet.

steps.title: Join the marks

steps.title: Repeat
steps.detail: Repeat the whole procedure and draw as many lines as you can. Together they represent the magnetic field around the magnet.

spec.question: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
options: Because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
Because field lines are always straight and straight lines never meet.
Because the magnetic field is zero at every crossing point.
Because field lines exist only inside the magnet.
spec.answer: Because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
spec.explanation: The direction of the field at a point is the direction in which the north pole of a compass needle would move there. A single point cannot give two directions, so two field lines cannot cross.
spec.expected_understanding: The student uses the definition of field direction to explain why field lines never cross.

spec.problem: A current through a horizontal power line flows in the east to west direction. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?

steps.title: Point the thumb
steps.detail: Hold the power line in your right hand so that your thumb points along the current, that is, from east to west.

steps.title: Curl the fingers
steps.detail: Your fingers wrap around the wire. They give the direction of the field lines in a plane perpendicular to the wire.

steps.title: Look from one end
steps.detail: Viewed from the east end, this curling is clockwise; viewed from the west end it is anti-clockwise.

steps.detail: Nothing changes at a point directly below or directly above the wire: the field still turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

spec.answer: At any point directly below or directly above the wire, the magnetic field turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

paragraphs: The displacement of the rod is largest, that is, the magnitude of the force is highest, when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field. In such a condition a simple rule gives the direction of the force.

Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand such that they are mutually perpendicular. If the first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the second finger in the direction of the current, then the thumb points in the direction of motion or the force acting on the conductor.

Remember that the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include the electric motor, the electric generator, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.

spec.problem: An electron moves horizontally towards the east and enters a magnetic field that points vertically upwards, at right angles to its motion. In which direction does the force acting on the electron point?

steps.title: Fix the field direction
steps.detail: The magnetic field points vertically upwards, so the forefinger of the left hand points up.

steps.title: Find the current direction
steps.detail: The electron moves towards the east. The direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons, so the current is towards the west. The second finger points west.

steps.title: Read the thumb
steps.detail: With the forefinger up and the second finger pointing west, the thumb of the left hand points towards the north.

steps.title: State the result
steps.detail: The force acts perpendicular to both the field and the current, so it is directed horizontally towards the north.

spec.answer: The force on the electron acts towards the north.

spec.question: A positively charged alpha-particle projected towards the west is deflected towards the north by a magnetic field. The direction of the magnetic field is
options: towards the south
towards the east
downward
upward
spec.answer: upward
spec.explanation: An alpha-particle is positively charged, so the current is towards the west. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the thumb must point north (the force) and the second finger west (the current); the forefinger then points upward, which is the direction of the field.
spec.expected_understanding: The student applies Fleming's left-hand rule to a moving positive charge and identifies the field direction.

spec.question: An electron moves horizontally towards the east. In which direction is the electric current taken?
options: Towards the west
Towards the east
Vertically upwards
Vertically downwards
spec.answer: Towards the west
spec.explanation: The direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of electrons. Since the electron moves towards the east, the current is taken towards the west.
spec.expected_understanding: The student recalls the convention that current direction is opposite to the direction of electron motion.

spec.question: You are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam moving horizontally from the back wall towards the front wall is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
options: vertically downwards
vertically upwards
towards the front wall
towards the back wall
spec.answer: vertically downwards
spec.explanation: The electrons move towards the front wall, so the current is taken in the opposite direction, towards the back wall. The force is to your right. With Fleming's left-hand rule, the thumb points right and the second finger points towards the back wall; the forefinger then points vertically downwards.
spec.expected_understanding: The student reverses the electron motion to get the current direction and then applies Fleming's left-hand rule in three dimensions.

spec.question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
options: When the current is parallel to the magnetic field.
When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
When the current in the conductor is zero.
When the conductor is kept outside the magnetic field.
spec.answer: When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
spec.explanation: The displacement of the rod in the activity, and so the magnitude of the force, is largest when the direction of the current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.
spec.expected_understanding: The student states the condition for the largest magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor.

spec.question: In Activity 12.7, the direction of the force acting on the current-carrying rod depends on which of the following?
options: Only the direction of the current.
Only the direction of the magnetic field.
Both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field.
Neither; the force has a fixed direction.
spec.answer: Both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field.
spec.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the direction of displacement, and changing the direction of the magnetic field by interchanging the poles also reverses the force. So the force direction depends on both the current direction and the field direction.
spec.expected_understanding: The student states that the direction of the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor depends on both the current direction and the magnetic field direction.

paragraphs: Electric power reaches a house through a main supply, either supported through overhead electric poles or by underground cables. One wire of this supply, usually with red insulation, is called the live wire (or positive). Another wire, with black insulation, is called the neutral wire (or negative). In our country the potential difference between the two is 220 V.

At the meter-board in the house these wires pass into an electricity meter through a main fuse, and through a main switch they are connected to the line wires in the house. Often two separate circuits are used: one of 15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as geysers and air coolers, and the other of 5 A current rating for bulbs and fans.

The earth wire has insulation of green colour and is usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house. It is a safety measure, especially for appliances that have a metallic body, for example an electric press, a toaster, a table fan or a refrigerator. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Any leakage of current to the metallic body then keeps its potential equal to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe electric shock.

paragraphs: In each separate circuit, different appliances can be connected across the live and neutral wires, and each appliance has a separate switch to switch the current on and off. In order that each appliance has equal potential difference, the appliances are connected in parallel to each other.

A fuse is an important component of all domestic circuits. It prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading. Overloading can occur when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact; this happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance. In such a situation the current in the circuit abruptly increases, and this is called short-circuiting. The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it to break the electric circuit and stop the flow of an unduly high current.
Overloading can also occur due to an accidental hike in the supply voltage, and sometimes it is caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket.

spec.problem: In a domestic circuit, the insulation of a wire gets damaged and the live wire comes into direct contact with the neutral wire. Explain what happens in the circuit and what the fuse does.

steps.title: Direct contact
steps.detail: The live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact. This is called short-circuiting.

steps.title: Current increases
steps.detail: Because of this direct contact, the current in the circuit abruptly increases.

steps.title: Fuse heats
steps.detail: The unduly high current causes Joule heating in the fuse.

steps.title: Circuit breaks
steps.detail: The Joule heating melts the fuse, which breaks the electric circuit and stops the flow of the unduly high current, preventing damage to the appliances and the circuit.

spec.answer: The damaged insulation causes short-circuiting: the live and neutral wires touch, the current abruptly increases, and the Joule heating melts the fuse, which breaks the circuit and prevents damage.

spec.question: At the time of a short circuit, the current in the circuit
options: reduces substantially.
does not change.
increases heavily.
varies continuously.
spec.answer: increases heavily.
spec.explanation: When the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact, the current in the circuit abruptly increases; this is called short-circuiting.
spec.expected_understanding: The student recalls the defining effect of a short circuit.

spec.question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
options: When the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact.
When the earth wire is connected to a metal plate in the ground.
When too many appliances are switched off at the same time.
When the supply voltage falls below 220 V.
spec.answer: When the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact.
spec.explanation: This happens when the insulation of wires is damaged or there is a fault in the appliance, and then the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
spec.expected_understanding: The student identifies the cause of short-circuiting.

spec.question: What is the function of an earth wire, and why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
options: It provides a low-resistance conducting path, so any leakage of current to the metallic body keeps its potential at that of the earth and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
It carries the working current to the appliance in place of the live wire.
It increases the current in the circuit so that the appliance works faster.
It converts the alternating supply into direct current for the appliance.
spec.answer: It provides a low-resistance conducting path, so any leakage of current to the metallic body keeps its potential at that of the earth and the user may not get a severe electric shock.
spec.explanation: The earth wire is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth. When the metallic body of an appliance is joined to it, a leakage current is taken safely to the earth instead of through the user.
spec.expected_understanding: The student explains earthing as a safety measure for appliances with a metallic body.

spec.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: A wire with a green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
options: True
False
spec.answer: False
spec.explanation: The wire with green insulation is the earth wire. The live wire usually has red insulation and the neutral wire has black insulation.
spec.expected_understanding: The student remembers the colour code of the three wires of a domestic supply.

spec.question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
options: The electric fuse and the earth wire.
The switch and the bulb.
The rheostat and the ammeter.
The magnet and the compass.
spec.answer: The electric fuse and the earth wire.
spec.explanation: The fuse melts and breaks the circuit when the current is unduly high, and the earth wire takes leakage current safely to the earth.
spec.expected_understanding: The student names the two safety devices described in the chapter.

spec.question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
options: Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket, and do not draw more current than the circuit's rating.
Connect all the appliances of the house in series.
Remove the fuse from the main board.
Disconnect the earth wire from the metallic appliances.
spec.answer: Do not connect too many appliances to a single socket, and do not draw more current than the circuit's rating.
spec.explanation: Overloading can be caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket, and also by an accidental hike in the supply voltage; the fuse is there to break the circuit if it happens.
spec.expected_understanding: The student connects everyday wiring habits with the cause of overloading.

paragraphs: An electric current always produces a magnetic field. Even the weak ion currents that travel along the nerve cells in our body produce magnetic fields. When you touch something, your nerves carry an electric impulse to the muscles you need to use, and this impulse produces a temporary magnetic field. Such fields are very weak, about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field.

The two main organs in the human body where the magnetic field produced is significant are the heart and the brain. The magnetic field inside the body forms the basis of obtaining images of different body parts by a technique called Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.

spec.question: Which technique uses the magnetic field inside the human body to obtain images of different body parts?
options: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
Short-circuiting.
Earthing.
The right-hand thumb rule.
spec.answer: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
spec.explanation: The magnetic field inside the body, which is significant in the heart and the brain, is the basis of obtaining images of body parts by MRI, and analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.
spec.expected_understanding: The student recalls one important medical use of magnetism described in the chapter.
